Business case, charter and project life cycle
business case|project charter|sponsor authorization|project life cycle
Before funding or starting a project, separate the case for investing from the authority to do the work.
Work with the sponsor to document the objective, constraints and authority needed to start. Use the business case to explain the investment; keep expected benefits visible as planning proceeds.
The instructor flags the life cycle and charter as study material. Identify the artifact by its purpose rather than by its format.
Use the charter to establish authority before using either a detailed predictive plan or an evolving backlog.
A business case justifies the investment. A charter authorizes the project. Neither is a detailed delivery plan.
business value|cost-benefit analysis|net present value|opportunity cost|success measures
Use this when choosing an investment or when stakeholders disagree about what success means.

Agree how stakeholders will measure outcomes. Compare costs with financial and nonfinancial benefits such as customer satisfaction. If comparing cash flows across periods, account for their timing and discount rate.
The instructor uses cost-benefit analysis to illustrate why a nonfinancial benefit can belong in the assessment.
A business case can justify a predictive project; incremental delivery gives an adaptive or hybrid project chances to check whether value is showing up.
A deliverable is an output. A benefit is an improvement expected from putting it to use. NPV is one appraisal technique, not a synonym for value.
Pick a way of working before committing stakeholders to the wrong kind of plan.
Use requirements stability and the need for feedback to choose how much planning to do up front. Revisit the choice when constraints or uncertainty change.
The instructor flags the comparison among predictive, adaptive and hybrid as study material. Read the scenario for constraints and uncertainty before picking an approach.
Predictive uses more up-front planning; adaptive refines work through feedback. Hybrid can mix the two where project conditions differ.
Adaptive planning still happens. Choosing an approach does not remove the need to plan or manage change.
hybrid delivery|fixed contractual milestones|evolving requirements|blended planning
hybrid project|blended approach|fixed dates and flexible scope
Use hybrid when part of the work needs fixed commitments and another part needs customer feedback.
Identify which milestones or scope are committed and what can evolve in the backlog. Agree how the team will report progress and who can approve changes that cross the boundary.
The course discusses a case with fixed contractual milestones and evolving requirements. Explain why both conditions matter before choosing hybrid.
Use predictive controls on committed work and adaptive planning where requirements evolve; coordinate milestones across both.
Calling a project hybrid does not make a contractual date optional or put every backlog change through a board.
go no-go review|stage gate|project management office
When moving between phases or making a decision beyond the team's authority, find out who can decide and what evidence they need.
Agree escalation thresholds and review points early. Take status, options and implications to the responsible decision maker. Use organizational policies and templates where they apply.
The instructor highlights phase boundaries and asks learners to distinguish what happens at a phase gate from regular reporting.

Predictive work may use formal phase gates. Adaptive work still follows governance and escalates decisions that exceed team authority; hybrid can combine iteration feedback with periodic governance review.
Visibility alone does not authorize an action. Escalation seeks a decision when it exceeds delegated authority.
Use the applicable ethics standard when project pressure conflicts with professional obligations.
Review the four values and distinguish mandatory standards from aspirational conduct. If the answer turns on a specific obligation, check the current Code and your applicable policies directly.
The instructor calls attention to the Code and the mandatory standards for each value. The transcript is a study lead, not a substitute for the Code.
Delivery approach does not change an ethical obligation. Tailor how you raise an issue to the applicable reporting channel.
An ethics obligation is different from a preferred leadership style or a convenient business outcome.
stakeholder register|stakeholder analysis|stakeholder engagement assessment matrix|current and desired engagement
Use this when starting a project, when someone new is affected or when support drops.

Start with the sponsor's contacts and ask who else might be affected, including outside the organization. Record stakeholders and compare their current engagement with what the project needs. Revisit the plan as relationships change.
The instructor separates stakeholder engagement from communications planning and points to a comparison slide. The transcript does not capture the slide's full contents.
Use planned engagement reviews in predictive work and feedback opportunities in adaptive work. In hybrid, keep one view of who needs engagement across the workstreams.
Stakeholder register|Stakeholder engagement assessment matrix|Stakeholder engagement plan
The register identifies stakeholders; an engagement plan describes how to work with them. Team members are stakeholders, but not every stakeholder is on the team.
When people receive late or conflicting information, agree who needs which update, how and when.
Ask stakeholders what they need to know and how they prefer to receive it. Use a feedback loop to check understanding, especially when decisions or handoffs depend on a message.
The instructor uses encode, decode and noise to illustrate a possible question design, not a confirmed exam item; the two-plan slide itself is not captured.
Formal reports and adaptive review conversations can coexist. Agree what each channel is for to avoid reporting the same information twice.
Communications management plan|Stakeholder engagement plan|Status report
Sending a message does not confirm understanding. Communications logistics differ from the work of gaining stakeholder support.
team charter|team norms|roles and responsibilities|Tuckman stages|team accountability
working agreements|ground rules|forming storming norming performing
Use this for a new team, after a membership change or when role expectations keep causing friction.
Create the working agreements with the team. Make responsibilities and behavioral expectations explicit; revisit the agreement when practice exposes a gap.
The instructor highlights team development and expectations. Use the team's behavior to reason about its stage instead of memorizing labels alone.
Use a shared set of working agreements across approaches; self-managing teams can agree how to work without the PM prescribing every decision.
The project charter authorizes the project; a team charter records how people will work together.
Use this when a team waits for permission on decisions it could own or when performance problems point to unmet needs.
Ask what is preventing the team from doing its work. Remove barriers, delegate within clear boundaries, and tailor your support to the team rather than taking over its decisions.
The course calls out autonomy and motivation. In a scenario, examine what support the team needs before adding control.
Adaptive teams emphasize self-management. Predictive and hybrid teams can also delegate decisions while keeping organizational accountability clear.
Empowerment needs decision boundaries. It is different from leaving a team without support.
conflict resolution|collaboration|conflict escalation|Leas levels of conflict
Use this when a disagreement begins to disrupt team decisions or relationships.
Find out what the parties disagree about and how severe it is. Help them acknowledge the problem and look for a resolution. Escalate when the severity or decision authority warrants it.
The instructor warns against ignoring conflict and uses Leas' levels as a study aid. Read the severity and context before selecting a response.
Use team working agreements and direct conversation across approaches. A retrospective can surface patterns, but active conflict may need attention before the next retro.
Collaboration is a way to work toward a resolution; escalation changes who must act or decide.
Use this when requirements are unclear or delivery teams cannot tell where a requirement came from.

Choose elicitation techniques for the stakeholders and question: interviews for individual detail, facilitated workshops for shared decisions, or observation to see the work. Record requirement sources and trace changes to downstream work.
The course reviews several elicitation techniques. Choose one based on the information and people in the scenario.

Predictive teams can maintain an explicit traceability matrix. Adaptive teams refine backlog items with stakeholders. Hybrid teams can keep traceability for commitments while refining implementation details.
A list of requirements does not show their origin, changes or verification unless it records those links.
Scope baseline and work breakdown structure
work breakdown structure|decomposition|work package|WBS dictionary|scope baseline
Use this when a deliverable is too large to estimate, assign or track as one piece.
Break deliverables into manageable work packages. Describe them in the WBS dictionary and check the decomposition against requirements before approving the scope baseline.
The instructor calls out the work package as the lowest level in the WBS. Recognize the difference between decomposition and sequencing.
Predictive work can use a scope baseline. Hybrid teams can apply it to defined deliverables while managing evolving work in a backlog. See the backlog topic for adaptive scope.
The WBS organizes deliverable scope. The schedule models activity sequence and timing.
Use this when new stakeholder feedback competes with already planned work.
Capture the need and discuss its value and consequences with stakeholders. The product owner orders the backlog so the team knows which work to consider next.
The course compares a predictive scope baseline to an evolving backlog. Identify who owns the ordering and whether the work actually changes a governed commitment.
Adaptive work uses backlog ordering and refinement. Hybrid can use a backlog within the parts of scope that may evolve, subject to contractual or baseline boundaries.
A request entering the backlog does not mean it is committed for delivery. Backlog refinement is distinct from approving a baseline change.
Quality management and cost of quality
quality management|cost of quality|prevention|appraisal|failure costs|continuous improvement
Use this when deciding where to spend effort to prevent defects or how to address repeated quality problems.
Agree how quality will be measured. Compare the cost of preventive work and appraisal with the cost of failures and rework. Use recurring defects as input to improving the process.
The course calls out cost of quality and compares quality responsibilities across approaches. Classify the activity before deciding which category of cost it belongs to.
A predictive plan can specify checks and responsibilities. In adaptive work, quality checks can be built into the team's definition of done. Hybrid teams may add separate contractual acceptance.
Quality management plan|Quality metrics|Test results|Definition of done
Inspection finds defects; preventive work aims to keep them from occurring. Quality management is broader than obtaining sign-off.
Acceptance criteria and definition of done
acceptance criteria|definition of done|deliverable verification|increment quality
Use this before work starts so people agree how to tell that a deliverable is acceptable and complete.

Write acceptance criteria for the item or deliverable. Agree which common quality checks the team applies before counting an increment as done. Confirm who accepts the deliverable when formal approval is required.
Session 5 notes that teams may distinguish the terms and offers simplified exam advice. Treat that as instructor guidance; use the scenario and do not infer a guaranteed PMI equivalence.
Predictive work often uses deliverable acceptance criteria. Adaptive work can pair item-level criteria with a shared definition of done. Hybrid teams may also need contractual sign-off.
Acceptance criteria|Definition of done|Test evidence|Acceptance record
Meeting internal completion checks is different from obtaining formal stakeholder acceptance.
